comparison: Both evaluations support the foundational inflammasome activation data (C1-C10, C17-C19). OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches and genetic specificity. Peer reviewers accepted these findings as the manuscript foundation with no concerns raised. High agreement on SUPPORTED status.

OpenEval finds C11-C16 SUPPORTED, emphasizing Signal II-specific mechanism. Peer review marks C14-C15 as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 challenging the interpretation that GB111 doesn't impair inflammasome-independent cytokines, noting dose-dependent IL-6 inhibition. Significant disagreement on the specificity claims.

Both evaluations address SAR data (C20-C28) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes clear structure-function relationships. Peer reviewers accepted the data but requested additional inactive control probes to strengthen the covalent mechanism evidence. Agreement on support with minor requests for enhancement.

OpenEval finds target identification (C29-C31) SUPPORTED with well-designed competition proteomics. Peer review marks overlapping claims (C30-C31, C46-C57) as UNCERTAIN, with reviewers finding data 'difficult to follow,' requesting quantitative analysis, mutational validation, and binding site mapping. Major disagreement on adequacy of target validation.

OpenEval R4 addresses C29 (cathepsin exclusion) which peer R5 also evaluates. OpenEval finds the competition proteomics well-designed. Peer reviewers question whether published inhibitors used in validation are properly validated and note GB-IA still shows activity against α-enolase. Partial overlap with different concerns.

Both address validation using structurally dissimilar inhibitors (C32-C45). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED and compelling. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, questioning inhibitor selectivity/validation, noting ENOblock produces different effects than GB111/KA, and observing GB-IA retains some α-enolase activity. Significant disagreement on validation quality.

OpenEval R6 addresses biochemical target engagement (C46-C57) and finds multiple lines of evidence SUPPORTED. Peer R4 covers overlapping claims and marks them UNCERTAIN, requesting quantitative concentration-dependent analysis and mutational validation. Disagreement on sufficiency of biochemical evidence.

Both address metabolic characterization showing disrupted glycolysis (C59-C71). OpenEval finds comprehensive evidence SUPPORTED. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, requesting validation that kinetics/extent of inflammasome activation match between conditions, noting differential ENOblock behavior, and asking if NAD+/NADH ratios can be directly manipulated. Disagreement on mechanistic validation completeness.

Both address metabolic rescue experiments (C72-C86). OpenEval finds dose-dependent effects and metabolic parameter restoration SUPPORTED as demonstrating causal relationship. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, requesting critical validation that metabolites reverse NAD+/NADH ratio changes. Agreement on data quality but disagreement on mechanistic proof completeness.

Both address mitochondrial ROS as proximal signal (C87-C91, C94). OpenEval finds the rotenone experiments and ROS data SUPPORTED with sound mechanistic logic. Peer reviewers also find these claims SUPPORTED with no concerns raised. High agreement on ROS mechanism.

Both address K+ efflux controls and ASC foci (C92-C93, C95). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED as distinguishing between NLRP3 activation mechanisms. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN due to low signal (5% ASC foci), requesting additional readouts like LDH release or IL-1β secretion for confirmation. Disagreement on signal robustness.

Both address Salmonella infection recapitulating metabolic disruption (C96-C107, C124). OpenEval finds correlations with MOI and timing SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find these claims SUPPORTED, accepting the glycolytic disruption model with no concerns raised. High agreement on infection data.

Both address metabolic rescue mechanism in bacterial infection (C108-C120). OpenEval finds genetic specificity and mechanistic links SUPPORTED. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, noting low IL-1β levels (80 to 40 pg/mL drop 'not exceptionally convincing'), discrepancy with published literature, and requesting tests of whether pyruvate/glutamine prevent Salmonella-induced NLRP3 activation. Disagreement on effect magnitude and mechanistic validation.

Both address summary/conclusion statements (C125-C129). OpenEval finds conclusions well-supported by comprehensive experimental evidence. Peer reviewers agree the manuscript reports novel findings of sufficient general interest and accept the core conceptual framework, though specific experimental details require strengthening. Agreement on overall significance despite concerns about specific experiments.

OpenEval R12 includes summary claims C121-C122 about NAD+/NADH ratio as trigger. Peer R6 addresses overlapping metabolic claims and requests direct manipulation of NAD+/NADH ratios to test if this mimics or overrides GB111 effects. Minor overlap with peer reviewers requesting additional mechanistic validation.

OpenEval R12 includes summary claim C123 about metabolic rescue. Peer R7 addresses metabolic rescue experiments and requests validation that metabolites reverse NAD+/NADH ratio changes. Minor overlap with peer reviewers seeking stronger mechanistic links.
OpenEval R12 includes summary claim C124 about Salmonella. Peer R10 addresses Salmonella infection data and finds them SUPPORTED. Minor overlap with both evaluations accepting the infection model.

OpenEval R2 includes C16 (Signal II specificity) which peer R1 also covers. OpenEval finds Signal II-specific mechanism SUPPORTED. Peer R1 accepts foundational data but peer R2 separately challenges the specificity interpretation for related claims. Minimal direct overlap but related conceptual concerns.
